name: Dr.Kegel
tagline: Quiz-funnel subscription app that hands you a guided pelvic floor exercise program with timed contract/relax sets and progress tracking.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Pricing sits behind a quiz funnel, so the number you see depends on the funnel.

verdictSummary: Strip the funnel and this is an interval timer with a progression schedule and a streak counter. The exercise protocol itself is not proprietary: hold, release, repeat, add seconds and reps over weeks, and every physio handout on the internet says roughly the same thing. What you are paying for is the packaging: a quiz that makes a generic plan feel prescribed to you, plus daily nudges that actually get you to do it. An agent can produce a local timer app with a multi-week ramp, haptics or audio cues, and a calendar heatmap in one sitting, and it will work offline forever with no card on file. The hard part is not the software, it is doing the sets.
coreLoopDIY: A local PWA that runs timed contract/relax sets from a multi-week progression schedule, cues each phase with sound and vibration, and logs completed sessions to a streak calendar.
requirements: a phone to install the PWA to the home screen for offline use and vibration
notification permission if you want daily reminders
whatYouLose: The onboarding quiz that makes a stock program feel personalized to your symptoms
Reliable push reminders: web notifications on iOS are flaky compared to a native app
Any pretense of clinical review, and the educational articles bundled alongside the timer
Guided voice coaching and the polished animations that help you keep rhythm
Health app / wearable sync and cross-device history
moatNotes: The real moat here is paid acquisition, not product. Winning a brand search auction is a distribution skill, and it does not survive you writing your own timer.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a subscription is a commitment device. Paying money and getting a plan with your name on it does more for adherence than a perfect timer you built yourself and stopped opening on day four. There is also genuine reassurance value in a product that looks medical and tells you the exercises are safe and correct, especially for people dealing with postpartum or post-surgical issues who do not want to freelance it. None of that is code, but it is not nothing.
notes: If you have actual symptoms, see a pelvic floor physio once and then use whatever timer you like, including one you wrote yourself.
prompt:
Build a local-first pelvic floor exercise trainer as an installable PWA. No accounts, no backend, no analytics, no network calls at all.

Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, vite-plugin-pwa for the service worker and manifest. All state in localStorage via a single typed store module. No database, no auth, no third-party SDKs.

Features, in scope:
1. A one-time setup screen: current level (beginner, intermediate, advanced), preferred session time of day, sessions per day (1-3).
2. A hardcoded 8-week progression table in a single TS file, one entry per week per level, each with: hold seconds, release seconds, reps, sets, rest between sets. Beginner starts around 3s hold / 5s release / 10 reps and ramps to longer holds and more reps. Keep the numbers in one exported const so they are trivial to edit.
3. A session runner: full-screen timer with a large expanding/contracting circle for the current phase, phase label (Squeeze / Relax / Rest), rep counter, set counter, and total time remaining. Cue each phase change with a short WebAudio beep (different pitch for squeeze vs relax) and navigator.vibrate when available. Pause, resume, and abandon controls.
4. On completion, write a session record (date, week, level, reps done, duration) to localStorage.
5. A home screen showing today's prescribed session, current week, current streak, and a 12-week calendar heatmap of completed sessions.
6. Settings: toggle sound, toggle vibration, adjust reminder time, export all data as JSON, import JSON, wipe all data.
7. Optional daily reminder using the Notifications API plus a service worker showNotification when the app is open or recently active. Ask permission only when the user enables reminders. Do not pretend this is reliable on iOS; put one plain sentence in settings saying home-screen install is required and delivery is not guaranteed.

Out of scope: any server, any login, HealthKit or Google Fit sync, video content, medical advice text beyond a single static disclaimer screen stating this is not a medical device and to consult a clinician for symptoms.

Requirements: works fully offline after first load, dark mode by default, thumb-reachable controls, keeps the screen awake during a session using the Screen Wake Lock API with a graceful fallback. Ship a README with run and build commands and a note on where to edit the progression table. If any secret were ever needed it goes in .env, but this build needs none.
